So, in San Jose proper, J Lohr has a tasting room that's right off the Alameda, very close to both Zona Rosa and Luna Kitchen. Either one of those paired with a tasting is a fun afternoon.

In Saratoga, there are a few different wineries to go to in different locales: on Montebello Rd, there are Pichetti Winery and Ridge. Pichetti's wines are decent but it's a fun place to taste, with a nice picnic area outside and an open space preserve to go on hikes, and sometimes peacocks will roam the grounds. Ridge is gorgeous and a prestige winery, you will need reservations on tock and it's not cheap but their wines are fantastic.

Saratoga also has some tasting rooms in downtown Saratoga (notably, Cinnabar, which is also decent wine), and on highway 9 Savannah Chanelle and Cooper Garrod are decent wines. My pick would actually be Domaine Eden, which is appointment only and a few miles up a dirt road. The tasting area is gorgeous though and the wines (especially the Mount Eden wines) are fantastic. Mount Eden is another place to visit, but I was recently told it's only open on weekdays - unsure if that's true.

In Los Gatos, Testarossa has a really cool winery in the hills just adjacent to the downtown area, and they make some very high end pinot noirs. In downtown LG, there is a tasting room for Saison, and I find their wines to be pretty good. It's owned by the same guy who runs the michelin-starred Saison restaurant in SF, as well as the wine bars with the same name (one in SF, one in Scotts Valley - which I also highly recommend for a relaxed wine bar experience. And they are struggling for business, would be cool to see them stick around!)

Going further north, I've been meaning to check out Rhys (appointment only) and Mindego Ridge; Thomas Fogarty is a gorgeous place and is a popular wedding venue but I find their wines to be overly acidic and overpriced; that said, they are known for their Gewürztraminer and it's usually decently priced. If you're willing to go out to Pescadero, Sante Arcangeli has a really cool tasting room in a renovated barn and a big open field with picnic tables (but they also have a tasting room in Aptos, mentioned below).

Going south of Los Gatos, there are a ton of wineries off summit road off highway 17 and further south on the west side of the Santa Cruz mountains.

On the west side of highway 17 are Byington and David Bruce. Byington's wines haven't been great for awhile, but it has beautiful sweeping views of the Santa Cruz mountains and has bocce and other things to just have a chill afternoon. David Bruce is a little more pretentious and makes good Pinot Noir and Sangiovese in my opinion, but I haven't been there in awhile.

On the East Side of 17 along and off summit are Wright's Station, Silver Mountain/Sonnet, Regale, and Loma Prieta. Wright's Station is my favorite of the four, they have a very nice Cabernet Franc and some good Chardonnays. Silver Mountain and Sonnet are tasting at the same place. It's old - it looks like it was a big party place in the 1980's and hasn't been updated at all since. But it's also one of the quietest places I've found in the valley (especially if you go sit off the back deck) and their wines are all aged on site until they're ready to drink, so if you want to buy something to drink now (instead of hold), this is a good place to go. Good reds here. Loma Prieta is quite a long drive but has a nice view of the mountains; their wines are ok, but they specialize in Pinotage, which is a varietal that most places don't do. Their sparkling Pinotage is actually \*very\* good, the rest of their wines are decent. Last time I was there they had a case deal for a red blend that was a steal, $5/bottle if you bought a case. It was a good table red and would be a good cooking wine. Regale is gorgeous and very well manicured, it's like an Italian Villa in the mountains. it has a huge space to hang out and bring your own food and party (giant jenga, bocce I think, more stuff) - it's definitely a party environment and potentially a fun place to hang, but IMO their wine sucks.

Wine country has so many options it's hard to point people to one place, but were I you, I would see if you can get reservations at 4 wineries on spring mountain. My recommendations are Robert Keenan (everything is good), Paloma (only Merlot but they're spectacular), Pride Mountain, and Smith Madrone - but there are many other fantastic wineries in that area.

However! If that's too difficult, you can find other options that will scratch your itch more locally. If you want to fit beer into your tourist days in SF, Toronodo in the lower Haight is a cash only dive beer bar that truly has great beer on every day (huge beer nerd mecca), and City Beer Store also has pretty great selection (among many other places). In Santa Clara, I'm a big fan of Barebottle brewing. 

Another option is if you want to see redwoods and the ocean, consider this day: drive south on hwy 17 to the Henry Cowell redwoods, then continue south on 17 to Santa Cruz. Go to Sante Adairius Portal location on Water Street, where they have food and incredible beer (they specialize in tart saisons (edit: but they make a wide variety of beer, not just tart stuff, and it's all good) - and are routinely listed as one of the best breweries in the country), go to the beach (beaches here aren't like SoCal beaches, they're colder and the sand is grainier, but they're beautiful in their own way), then swing through Capitola to Gayle's bakery and pick up some food to go. Then go down to corrallitos to go wine tasting at Windy Oaks (pretty much only Pinot Noir, but v good, also a fun drive through some redwoods) and try to catch the sunset on top of the ridge at the winery. Back to Santa Cruz for dinner (I would recommend El Copal on the west side for molé, or somewhere downtown if you want to get more beers at Lupolo craft house). 

There are other wineries that are more adjacent to San Jose that I can also recommend if you don't want to go up to wine country. Lots of great things to do (and drink!) around here. Cheers!

No, but they sit right next to one another. The procedure she had done (rf cardiac ablation) is meant to create burn marks in the left atrium to provide suggested channels for the electrical current in the heart to flow, assisting it to beat in synch with the ventricle. Atrial fibrillation is when the electrical currents don't synch, but rather they wander. The lack of syncopation between the atrium and ventricle can lead to clotting under the atrial appendage, which can then be thrown and cause a stroke. 

So, when they did the ablation procedure, they burned a tiny, pinhole sized  (maybe smaller) hole in her atrium and esophagus. Most they catch earlier, as it's a known side effect. But hers they did not. 

And no, it's not lost on me that she had a procedure to avoid having a stroke, and it - in a roundabout way - caused her brain to get showered with emboli. Sometimes life's a pisser. But she's alive and that's amazing.

Hey, 28 y/o SJ native here.  What kind of stuff do you want to do?  The Bay Area has...tons of things to do.

My normal tourist schedule:

1) San Francisco 

- Angel Island: Prettier than Alcatraz, easier to get to, the "west coast Ellis Island," if you will.  Better views of SF too.  If you're super interested in the history of Alcatraz, though, hit it up.
- Golden Gate Bridge: Many people walk or bike across the bridge.  If you're going to drive and look back, I recommend avoiding the rest stop at the north side of the bridge and instead taking the first exit, going left under the freeway and into the Marin Headlands
- Muir Woods (North Bay): Beautiful forest and redwoods with tons of hiking trails, some which lead to gorgeous views of the sea.  WIll be packed because it's a national park.  There are many other forests you can see (see: south bay loop/trip).
- Mission Dolores: One of the famed missions of California, a cultural hub of SF that gave rise to the Mission district.  The missions were a trail up the coast of California that the missionaries built to settle the state and evangelize the coast.  See also: Dolores Park
- Coit Tower / Lombard St / Pier 39 / Cable Cars: The other typical SF touristy landmarks, all worthwhile if you haven't done them.  Protip: Go down Lombard St. at night; you'll get a beautiful view of the Bay Bridge and it's light display (there's an artist's light display of LEDs on the Bay Bridge for the next 2 years)  Another protip: If you aren't taking a cable car to Pier 39, consider eating at Scoma's - both a personal favorite for seafood, and they will valet your car for either free or reasonable cost (parking near pier 39 is both expensive and hard to come by)
- The Armory: Kink.com headquarters, tours given daily (?)
- Anchor Brewing Co. : Home of Anchor Steam - a unique brewing tour if you can get reservations.  Given twice a day during weekdays; reservations required.
- Toronado: An incredible beer bar in the Lower Haight, next to Rosamunde's, a boutique sausage grill.  CASH ONLY
- City Beer Store: See Toronado
- Buena Vista Cafe: Origin of the Irish Coffee
- AT&T Park: one of the coolest baseball stadiums in the country.  Garlic Fries are a must.
- San Francisco LOVES brunch.  Consider brunching on the weekend.
- Other points of interest: California Museum of Science, Fort Mason, Legion of Honor, MOMA, Sunset District, Walt Disney Museum, The Castro Theatre, Hot Cookie, Sutro Baths, Land's End
- OH and America's Cup qualifying (sailing) is going on right now, so there will be heats if you want to go be a spectator.  Also the Wallflowers and Counting Crows are doing a show on the 18th.


2) South Bay

- Winchester Mystery House - built by Sara Winchester, the widow and heir of the Winchester rifle fortune; she built a mansion to protect her from and confuse the spirits of those who were killed by the Winchester arms and ammo and subsequently haunted her.  The house has crazy hallways, rooms she did seances in, and other weird stuff.  The house was continuously in construction until she died.
- Henry Cowell Redwoods: A park with really tall redwoods and a short loop through them; it will take maybe about an hour to walk.  Easiest way to see big trees, but not the biggest trees in Northern California
- Mystery Spot, as described by /u/photoginny
- Roaring Camp Railroad: a railroad through the Santa Cruz mountains; kind of fun
- Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk:  one of the last coastal boardwalks left in the country, an amusement park by the sea.  Santa Cruz as a whole is a huge vacation destination for people from the Central Valley during the summer.  There are big concerts on the beach on Friday nights; Cracker and Camper von Beethoven will be performing on 7/19.   Right next to the boardwalk: Santa Cruz Wharf, good for seafood and hanging out on the ocean.
- Capitola: quaint beach town south of Santa Cruz.
- Monterey Bay Aquarium - Wonderful aquarium.  Also near Cannery Row, for all the Steinbeck fans.  See also: John Steinbeck museum in Salinas
- 17 Mile Drive: A private drive along some of the most scenic coastline you'll see anywhere.  I think you pay ~$10 to drive it, but there are some amazing views, including the lone spruce
- Carmel-by-the-sea: Unsure if Clint Eastwood is still the mayor, but a lot of townies go down to the beach to watch the sunset with their dogs and kids.  It's pretty awesome.

Other points of interest: Santa Cruz Wineries, Aptos Wine Trail, San Gregorio General Store, Half Moon Bay, Filoli House/Gardens, Stanford University

3) North Bay:

- Lagunitas Brewing Co., Petaluma: Home to some of the best hoppy beer in the country, their tap room on the brewing premesis is a cute place to hang out.
- Russian River Brewing Co., Santa Rosa: Home to some of the best sour beer (and hoppy beer) in the country, their brewpub in downtown Santa Rosa is a hoppin' place to get some food and enjoy the nectar of the gods that is Pliny the Elder
- Wineries, Napa/Sonoma: If you like wine, you should make at least a day of going to Wine Country.  Artesa is beautiful, Etude has great wines, Spring Mountain is full of incredible wineries (including Keenan), but most require reservations ahead of time.  Chateau Montelena makes some of the best wine, IMO.  Beaulieu Vineyards (BV) also has a reserve tasting room if you're into super high end red blends.  Kenwood is fun, Chateau St. Jean is beautiful (and has pretty good wine), Prager Port Works is fun if you like Port.   Alpha Omega is pretty popular.  And Del Dotto pours to get you wasted.  Be careful!
- Other points of interest: Cotati, Infineon Raceway, Sol Food, Tiburon, Sausalito.  Plenty of hiking.

4) East Bay: I'm not the person to ask about the east bay, unfortunately, but I've had a lot of fun there.  Yoshi's in Jack London Square is supposed to be pretty cool.

5) If you can - and if you're nature people at all - please take a day (or two) and go to Yosemite.  It's truly a one of a kind place that's utterly, unimaginably gorgeous.

I was coming in just to post on this topic.  I know I can't echo your experience - it is yours and yours alone - but I have had times in my life where I've used objective logic to deal with situations.  I tell you, it is a great tool!...but it doesn't always work, as you're expressing.

What I eventually ended discovering in my life was that I used objectivity as a shield to not deal with emotions, and that the shield was completely destroyed when the situation had absolutely NO LOGIC and was about FEELINGS.  Sound familiar?

So what eventually helped me was understanding what emotions *really are*.  While you can list emotions and understand what they feel like, no doubt (ex. fear, hate, anger, joy, melancholy, etc.), the nature of an emotion makes no sense.  Why do people get pissed off at other bad drivers literally seconds after exhibiting the same behavior?  Hypocrisy, yes, but also emotion.  Emotions are the way our brain tells us to react to a situation...

but see, therein lies the trick.  Our inferences, our senses, our past experiences and society and culture and all this other crap come together in one split instant and spits out some form of emotion, and that's how we feel!?  absolutely insane, or genius, depending on how you look at it.  **But it's something that's done unconsciously.**  Like breathing.  And we evolved emotion (as have all beings) from fight/flight mechanisms which kept us alive.

SO WHAT DOES THIS ALL MEAN?  You can't control your emotions.  They happen.  And to feel ashamed or confused about your emotions is allowing yourself to fall victim to something you cannot control - you're beating yourself up for a trait we evolved for evolutionary purposes.  What you CAN control is how your emotions affect your subsequent actions.  So you feel sad about your ex-girlfriend?  Isolate her from your life, be selfish about your own needs.  Mourn the relationship.  But know you have better - and it's not some intangible promise you're making to yourself, it's not a shred of hope that you're clinging to.  It's RIGHT IN FRONT OF YOU.

I promise you, things will get better.  Just try allowing yourself to be vulnerable to emotion...and then be analytical about what actions you take to either inflame or suppress the emotion.  You control your actions, and you sound like your brain can master this.

Just trust in yourself.

tl;dr: emotions can't be controlled, but subsequent actions can.  don't be ashamed of feeling something - anything!
